name: Healthcare & Life Sciences AI
intro:
Healthcare and life sciences AI covers models and platforms built into clinical and biomedical workflows where the output touches patient care, a diagnosis, or a regulated data set: EHR-embedded tools like Epic's AI features, medical LLMs like Google's Med-PaLM and MedLM, drug discovery platforms like Insilico Medicine, healthcare analytics from Merative, and genomics-driven precision medicine from Tempus AI. It excludes general-purpose consumer chatbots used for health questions and enterprise AI platforms with no clinical specialization, since the governing constraint here is HIPAA, FDA device rules, and genetic privacy law rather than generic data protection.

A health system or life sciences buyer is choosing where in the workflow the AI sits. Epic's tools work inside the record a clinician already has open. Google's MedLM targets clinical reasoning as a standalone model layered onto existing systems. Merative serves population health and payer-side analytics rather than bedside decisions. Tempus AI and Insilico Medicine sit upstream, in oncology testing and molecular drug design, feeding a treatment or research decision.

Regulatory and deal activity moved fast this year. The FDA published a discussion paper in August 2026 proposing a two-axis risk framework for generative AI-enabled devices, addressing foundation models and agentic AI for the first time. Epic previewed Factory at HIMSS26 in March 2026, letting health systems build clinical AI agents on Epic's models. Tempus AI agreed in July 2026 to acquire Personalis for roughly $1.5 billion, folding molecular residual disease testing into its oncology platform.

Epic and Tempus AI are the clearest reference points for US health systems, given how deeply each is embedded in clinical and oncology workflows, with Google's MedLM the one to watch as a portable alternative not tied to a single EHR.

reading.body:
Healthcare AI vendors face overlapping regulatory burdens across data privacy, liability, and cross-border governance that create distinct operational friction points absent from consumer AI.

The tools listed span clinical decision support, medical language models, drug discovery, and genomic analysis. Each operates under different compliance frameworks. US-based clinical tools must navigate HIPAA, FDA software as a medical device rules, and diagnostic liability. Google's medical LLM requires business associate agreements and carries explicit liability exposure. Tempus handles genetic data under GINA constraints. Insilico Medicine, operating from Hong Kong, operates under different jurisdictional regimes entirely while handling sensitive molecular and clinical data that can flow across borders.

This fragmentation matters for AI infrastructure because healthcare AI cannot simply scale like consumer models. A clinical decision support system deployed in one health system cannot be trivially moved or retrained without re-certification. Data residency and HIPAA business associate requirements constrain where computation can occur and who can access training data. Drug discovery AI like Insilico's must balance IP generation across jurisdictions with data provenance tracking. These are not compute problems; they are governance problems that precede compute allocation.

The data covers vendor tooling and regulatory surface but does not address infrastructure requirements, power consumption, or the actual building footprints required to host these systems in compliant jurisdictions. It also does not show which tools actually run at scale in production versus research stage, or how frequently regulatory changes force retraining or redeployment cycles that consume additional compute.
